text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The government essentially said yes to Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), but said not right now. On a scale of one to five where five means a yes to EMU, the Social Democrats indicated a four in their statement on Tuesday, citing scepticism towards the European Union and the EMU project among Swedes as the reason for their decision.

- The managing director of Swedish utility company Sydkraft says he doubts a nuclear reactor at the group's Barseback plant will be shut down by July 1 next year. The government has said it plans to begin phasing out the country's nuclear power programme.
- Economists say Swedish households will have to pay through higher real interest rates if the country does not join EMU from its 1999 start.

- The door to EMU is open for Sweden -- but only after the year 1999. Prime Minister Goran Persson said low public opinion towards the project was behind the government's decision. A referendum on the issue can become a reality.

- Economics professor Lars Calmfors, who has worked as an advisor to the government on EMU, says it is good the government wants to retain its ability to negotiate on EMU. However, instead of referring to that the project is uncertain, a more logical argument to stay outside EMU would have been the fact that the Swedish economy is not ready for the currency union. High unemployment is the main reason, Calmfors says.

- Demand for managers with a salary of over $100,000 a year increased by 20 percent worldwide but fell by two percent in western Europe because of uncertainty over EMU and the British elections, a survey by Korn/Ferry Internationals shows.

- The government's decision to stay outside EMU could have been worse. The crown strengthened marginally on the news that Sweden is holding the door open but the first time the country could join EMU is in 2000.
- Swedish municipalities are standing in line at the door of the interior ministry to receive emergency financial aid. Together 11 municipalities need around 460 million crowns.
- Swedish telecoms group Ericsson is cutting off funds for high-speed computer research which had been carried out by the Swedish Institute of Computer Science.

- Restructuring costs trimmed the eight-month profit for chemicals and plastics group Perstorp. The group posted a pre-tax profit of 362 million crowns compared to 456 million in the period a year earlier.
